options.label: D
options.text: Consent of victim is sufficient, and that of legal guardian is not required for MTP if the girl is found to be pregnant at a later stage

questions.answerText: Consent of victim is sufficient, and that of legal guardian is not required for MTP if the girl is found to be pregnant at a later stage
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Consent of victim is sufficient, and that of legal guardian is not required for MTP if the girl is found to be pregnant at a later stage

 

According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, for minors (those under 18 years of age), the consent of the legal guardian is required for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). A 13-year-old girl cannot provide independent consent for MTP. While her consent for medical examination and treatment of injuries is sufficient, any decision regarding an abortion must involve her legal guardian.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Take a detailed history: This is correct and one of the first steps after a case of sexual violence is reported. Taking a thorough and sensitive history from the victim is crucial for both medical and legal purposes.

 

Option B. Preserve clothing: This is a correct course of action as the victim’s clothing may contain forensic evidence, such as biological material (e.g., semen, blood), which is critical for the investigation.

 

Option C. Consent of a legal guardian is not mandatory to give the medical treatment for injuries to the victim: This is correct. In cases of sexual violence, medical treatment for injuries can be given to a minor without the legal guardian's consent, as providing emergency care and addressing injuries is a priority.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For medical treatment following sexual violence, the consent of the victim is sufficient, but in cases involving minors, the legal guardian's consent is mandatory for MTP (Medical Termination of Pregnancy). Understanding the legal requirements for minors in medical situations is crucial for healthcare providers.

questions.stem: Identical twins have similarities in all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fingerprint pattern 

 

Although identical twins share the same genetic material (DNA), they do not have identical fingerprint patterns. Fingerprints are formed by both genetic and environmental factors in the womb, making them unique even between identical twins. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blood group: Identical twins have the same blood group since this is genetically determined.

 

Option B. DNA fingerprinting: Identical twins have the same DNA profile because they originate from the same fertilized egg, although very minor variations can occur due to mutations.

 

Option D. Iris color: Identical twins typically have the same iris color, as it is determined by their shared genetic makeup.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Identical twins have the same blood group, DNA, and often the same iris color, but their fingerprints are unique due to the influence of environmental factors during development.

questions.stemHtml: A child who is a victim under POCSO act is brought to the department of forensic medicine for age estimation. The X-ray image of the hand is shown below. What is the likely age of the child?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 13 years 

 

In the X-ray provided, you can observe the development of carpal bones. The pisiform bone is of particular importance here as it is the last carpal bone to ossify and typically appears after 10 years of age, most often between 10 to 12 years. Given the appearance of the pisiform in the X-ray, the child is likely older than 10 years, making the most appropriate age estimation 13 years.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 4 years: At 4 years of age, only a few carpal bones would have ossified, and the pisiform would not have appeared yet.

 

Option B. 7 years: At this age, more carpal bones would be ossified, but the pisiform would still not be present.

 

Option C. 8 years: Similar to 7 years, the pisiform bone would not yet have appeared.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In forensic age estimation using hand X-rays, the appearance of carpal bones is a key indicator. The pisiform bone is the last carpal bone to ossify, and its appearance suggests that the child is at least 10 to 12 years old. In this case, the most likely age is 13 years based on the full set of carpal bones observed.

questions.stem: A rape victim is examined in a hospital and a specimen from her vagina is subjected to staining by 10% HCl, potassium iodide, iodine and water. Dark brown rhombic shaped crystals appear immediately. Which confirmatory test should be done, if the accused is azoospermic?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Acid phosphatase test 

 

The Florence test is the test described in the question, which is a presumptive test for semen. It detects the presence of choline by producing brown rhombic crystals when the sample is treated with iodine solution. However, since the accused is azoospermic (meaning he does not produce sperm), sperm cells will not be present in the sample. Therefore, a different confirmatory test must be used to detect semen components that are present regardless of sperm.

 

The acid phosphatase test is a reliable and widely used confirmatory test for the presence of seminal fluid, even in cases where sperm are absent (e.g., azoospermic individuals). Acid phosphatase is an enzyme produced by the prostate gland and is present in high concentrations in seminal fluid, making it a useful indicator in such cases.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Barberio test: This test is used to detect the presence of spermine, which is found in semen. However, it is not specific enough to be a confirmatory test for semen when sperm is absent.

 

Option C. Florence test: This is the presumptive test described in the question. While it detects choline in semen, it is not a confirmatory test and has already been performed.

 

Option D. Creatine Phosphokinase test: This test detects an enzyme found in sperm, but since the accused is azoospermic, this test would not be useful in confirming the presence of semen.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: During a high-profile court case, the jury is presented with the situation of a 40-year-old university professor who has been charged with the serious assault of a colleague. It comes to light during the trial that the professor has been battling untreated schizophrenia, characterized by profound auditory hallucinations and delusions. On the day in question, he was under the delusion that his colleague was a covert agent sent to harm him, leading to the assault. The defence argues that the professor's mental state at the time of the incident rendered him incapable of understanding his actions' nature or distinguishing right from wrong. Given these circumstances and applying the Legal Test of Insanity, how should the professor's criminal responsibility be assessed?

options.label: A
options.text: He is criminally responsible because he was conscious of his physical actions during the assault.

options.label: B
options.text: He is not criminally responsible due to his inability to comprehend the true nature of his actions because of his delusional perception.

options.label: C
options.text: He is not criminally responsible due to his inability to control his actions due to his underlying schizophrenia.

options.label: D
options.text: He is criminally responsible because his mental illness does not excuse violent behavior.

questions.answerText: He is not criminally responsible due to his inability to comprehend the true nature of his actions because of his delusional perception.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) He is not criminally responsible due to his inability to comprehend the true nature of his actions because of his delusional perception.

 

The Legal Test of Insanity, often referred to as the McNaughton Rule, focuses on whether a defendant was capable of understanding the nature and quality of their act or distinguishing between right and wrong at the time of the offense. In this case, the professor, due to untreated schizophrenia and a profound delusional belief that his colleague was a threat, was unable to comprehend the reality of his actions. Therefore, his mental state meets the criteria for legal insanity, which absolves him of criminal responsibility.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. He is criminally responsible because he was conscious of his physical actions during the assault: While the professor may have been physically conscious of his actions, the legal test for insanity focuses on understanding, not just physical awareness. The professor’s delusions distorted his perception, preventing him from recognizing the true nature of his actions.

 

Option C. He is not criminally responsible due to his inability to control his actions due to his underlying schizophrenia: Legal insanity in this context does not primarily focus on whether the defendant could control their actions but rather whether they understood the nature of their actions and could differentiate right from wrong. Schizophrenia, by itself, does not automatically lead to an inability to control actions under the law.

 

Option D. He is criminally responsible because his mental illness does not excuse violent behavior: Mental illness, when severe enough to impair one’s ability to understand the nature of their actions or the morality of those actions, can absolve an individual of criminal responsibility. Therefore, this option is incorrect, as his mental illness, specifically his delusions, did render him unable to understand his actions.

 

Educational Objective:

In this case, the professor’s schizophrenia and resulting delusions impaired his understanding, leading to a conclusion of no criminal responsibility due to legal insanity.

questions.stem: In a rural clinic, a medical officer is faced with a case of acute poisoning. A 25-year-old patient has been brought in after ingesting an unknown substance at home. The medical officer needs to quickly administer an initial treatment to reduce the absorption of the poison. In preparing an emergency response, the medical officer considers the components of the universal antidote. Which of the following substances, commonly available in medical settings, is a part of this universal antidote and should be administered in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Activated charcoal

 

The universal antidote is an old concept consisting of several components aimed at reducing the absorption of ingested poisons. The most important and effective component of modern universal antidotes is activated charcoal, which binds many toxins and prevents their absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. It is widely used in cases of poisoning due to its broad effectiveness against a variety of substances.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Copper sulfate is not part of the universal antidote and is rarely used today due to its own toxicity.

 

Option C and Option D. Egg white and starch were once considered parts of certain antidotal mixtures for specific types of poisonings, such as heavy metals, but they are not components of the universal antidote.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of unknown poisoning, activated charcoal is the most commonly used component of the universal antidote due to its ability to adsorb a wide range of toxins and prevent further absorption. It is important to initiate its use promptly in emergency poisoning cases.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old industrial worker was found dead at work place. He was working in a confined space near a decaying organic material storage facility for several hours since morning. Likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Methane 

 

The worker was in a confined space near decaying organic material, which can produce sewer gases—a mixture of gases including methane, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide. Methane, a colorless and odorless gas, is a common byproduct of decaying organic matter, especially in confined spaces like sewage systems or storage facilities for decomposing organic material. Methane displaces oxygen in the air, leading to suffocation in poorly ventilated areas. Since it is not toxic in small amounts, but lethal in high concentrations due to oxygen displacement, it is the most likely cause of death in this scenario.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. CO (Carbon Monoxide): Carbon monoxide is produced in fire-related environments and involves incomplete combustion of carbon-containing materials. It is not typically associated with decaying organic matter or confined spaces unless there is a source of combustion, which is not described in this scenario.

 

Option B. CN (Cyanide): Cyanide gas is extremely toxic and typically associated with fires or industrial chemical processes. It is not released by decaying organic materials and is therefore an unlikely cause in this case.

 

Option D. Methemoglobin: Methemoglobinemia occurs when hemoglobin is oxidized, leading to a reduced ability to carry oxygen. This condition is usually caused by exposure to certain drugs or chemicals, not by exposure to decaying organic material.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methane is a common gas produced by decaying organic matter in confined spaces, and it poses a significant risk due to its ability to displace oxygen. Recognizing the risk of methane and other sewer gases in such environments is essential for preventing occupational hazards in confined spaces.

This condition is usually caused by exposure to certain drugs or chemicals, not by exposure to decaying organic material. Educational Objective: Methane is a common gas produced by decaying organic matter in confined spaces, and it poses a significant risk due to its ability to displace oxygen. Recognizing the risk of methane and other sewer gases in such environments is essential for preventing occupational hazards in confined spaces.

questions.stem: 18-year woman is having agitation, hallucinations, and nystagmus. She is also exhibiting muscle rigidity & occasional catatonic posturing. Likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Phencyclidine

 

The symptoms described—agitation, hallucinations, nystagmus, muscle rigidity, and catatonic posturing—are classic signs of Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication. PCP, also known as "angel dust," is a dissociative hallucinogen that can produce severe agitation, vivid hallucinations, muscle rigidity, and nystagmus (rapid involuntary eye movements), which are characteristic of PCP intoxication. Catatonic posturing and muscle rigidity are also commonly associated with PCP use, making it the most likely cause in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Amphetamines: While amphetamines can cause agitation and hyperactivity, they do not typically cause nystagmus, muscle rigidity, or catatonic posturing. Hallucinations may occur, but the overall symptom profile described fits PCP intoxication better.

 

Option B. Cocaine: Cocaine can cause agitation and hallucinations, but nystagmus and muscle rigidity are not typical of cocaine use. Cocaine tends to cause more intense euphoria, tachycardia, and dilated pupils rather than the specific symptoms described.

 

Option C. LSD: LSD is a potent hallucinogen that can cause vivid hallucinations, but it is not associated with nystagmus or muscle rigidity. LSD tends to cause visual hallucinations and altered perceptions without the severe agitation or physical rigidity seen in PCP intoxication.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication can cause a combination of symptoms, including agitation, hallucinations, nystagmus, muscle rigidity, and catatonic posturing. These signs, particularly the presence of nystagmus and muscle rigidity, help differentiate PCP from other hallucinogenic or stimulant substances. Recognizing these specific symptoms is essential in diagnosing PCP intoxication.

questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old child from an environment presents with pallor, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Laboratory investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear demonstrates a peculiar finding shown below. Which of the following differential diagnoses is most likely responsible for this finding in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Viral infection affecting erythropoiesis, causing aberrant RNA synthesis.

options.label: B
options.text: Lead poisoning leading to abnormal iron metabolism, leading to intracellular iron accumulation within red blood cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, caused by the production of autoantibodies against red blood cell antigens.

options.label: D
options.text: Lead poisoning affecting heme synthesis and resulting in aggregates of ribosomal material within red blood cells.

questions.answerText: Lead poisoning affecting heme synthesis and resulting in aggregates of ribosomal material within red blood cells.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lead poisoning affecting heme synthesis and resulting in aggregates of ribosomal material within red blood cells.

 

The image shows basophilic stippling of red blood cells (RBCs), which is a characteristic finding in cases of lead poisoning. Lead poisoning inhibits key enzymes involved in heme synthesis, such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase. This results in defective heme production and accumulation of heme precursors, which leads to microcytic hypochromic anemia. Additionally, lead poisoning interferes with the degradation of ribosomal RNA in developing red blood cells, causing ribosome aggregation, which appears as basophilic stippling on a blood smear.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Viral infection affecting erythropoiesis, causing aberrant RNA synthesis: Viral infections can disrupt erythropoiesis but do not typically lead to the basophilic stippling seen here. Viral infections are more likely to result in a normocytic anemia without the ribosomal aggregation characteristic of lead poisoning.

 

Option B. Lead poisoning leading to abnormal iron metabolism, leading to intracellular iron accumulation within red blood cells: Lead poisoning does not cause iron accumulation inside red blood cells. Instead, it affects heme synthesis by inhibiting enzymes, leading to microcytic anemia and basophilic stippling, but without iron overload in the RBCs.

 

Option C. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, caused by the production of autoantibodies against red blood cell antigens: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia usually presents with spherocytes or evidence of red cell destruction on a smear but does not result in basophilic stippling.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of lead poisoning, enzymes involved in heme synthesis are inhibited, leading to basophilic stippling on a blood smear due to the accumulation of ribosomal material in red blood cells. This is a key diagnostic feature and should prompt further investigation for lead exposure, especially in children from environments where such exposure is common.

questions.stem: 58 yr woman comes to emergency with blue skin, and headache. She does not complain of chest pain or dyspnoea. She Recently started on isosorbide nitrite 40 mg QID. Vitals normal, markedly cyanotic, has laboured respiration. 100% O2 does not help. Cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Methemoglobinemia

 

This patient's presentation is consistent with methemoglobinemia, which can be induced by certain drugs like isosorbide dinitrate. In methemoglobinemia, hemoglobin is oxidized to form methemoglobin (Fe³⁺), which cannot effectively bind and release oxygen. As a result, the tissues do not receive adequate oxygen, leading to cyanosis, despite normal oxygen levels in the blood. Since methemoglobin does not release oxygen efficiently, administration of 100% oxygen does not correct the cyanosis. Symptoms like headache, cyanosis, and lack of response to oxygen therapy are typical in this condition.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cyanide poisoning: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome C oxidase, preventing cells from using oxygen. However, cyanide poisoning usually results in cherry-red skin due to increased oxygen levels in venous blood, rather than cyanosis. It also typically presents with more severe systemic toxicity, such as confusion, seizures, or respiratory distress.

 

Option B. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning: CO binds to hemoglobin, forming carboxyhemoglobin, which prevents oxygen from binding. CO poisoning causes cherry-red skin rather than cyanosis, and the patient typically experiences symptoms such as dizziness, headache, and shortness of breath. However, 100% oxygen usually helps improve the condition, unlike in this case.

 

Option D. Myocardial infarction: While myocardial infarction can cause symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypoxia, it is less likely to cause the specific cyanosis and labored breathing without pain, especially in the context of recent nitrate use and lack of improvement with 100% oxygen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methemoglobinemia is caused by the oxidation of hemoglobin to methemoglobin (Fe³⁺), which impairs oxygen delivery to tissues. It can be induced by drugs like isosorbide dinitrate and presents with cyanosis and headache, with no improvement after oxygen therapy. Recognizing this condition is important, as the treatment typically involves administration of methylene blue, which reduces methemoglobin back to functional hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old male presents to ED in a coma with CPR in progress. A friend found him in the schoolyard. His friend confesses that the patient has been depressed over the past several days. His initial labs reveal hypocalcemia and a severe metabolic acidosis. The urine shows calcium oxalate crystals. What was the toxic ingestion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ethylene Glycol

 

The presence of calcium oxalate crystals in the urine, along with hypocalcemia and metabolic acidosis, strongly suggests ethylene glycol poisoning. Ethylene glycol is metabolized in the body into toxic metabolites, including glycolic acid and oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium in the body to form calcium oxalate crystals, which can be seen in the urine and may lead to acute renal failure. The binding of oxalic acid to calcium also causes hypocalcemia, further contributing to the patient's symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Methanol: Methanol poisoning can also cause metabolic acidosis, but it is typically associated with visual disturbances (such as "snow blindness") due to the formation of formic acid. Methanol poisoning does not cause calcium oxalate crystals or hypocalcemia.

 

Option C. Organophosphates: Organophosphate poisoning typically presents with symptoms of cholinergic excess, such as salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, and muscle twitching (SLUDGE syndrome). It is not associated with metabolic acidosis, hypocalcemia, or calcium oxalate crystals.

 

Option D. Ethanol: Ethanol intoxication can cause metabolic acidosis (due to alcohol-induced ketoacidosis), but it does not cause calcium oxalate crystals or hypocalcemia. Ethanol is metabolized to acetaldehyde and acetic acid, which are not associated with these findings.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ethylene glycol poisoning leads to the production of oxalic acid, which binds to calcium and forms calcium oxalate crystals. This results in hypocalcemia, severe metabolic acidosis, and potential acute renal failure. Recognizing these characteristic findings is crucial for diagnosing ethylene glycol poisoning and initiating appropriate treatment, which includes fomepizole or ethanol to inhibit further metabolism of ethylene glycol.

questions.stem: An approximately twenty-something year old female presents to the emergency department after she collapsed outside a bar. Physical Examination: T: 97.5°F HR: 60 bpm RR: 5 breaths per minute BP: 75/57 mm Hg Pupils are miotic but equal. Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation. CV: Regular rate and rhythm. Abdomen: Normal Neurologic: GCS = 6 (E1V1M4). Best treatment?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Naloxone

 

This patient presents with a very low respiratory rate (5 breaths per minute), low blood pressure, constricted (miotic) pupils, and depressed mental status (GCS of 6). These findings are characteristic of opioid overdose. Opioids can cause profound respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and altered consciousness, as seen in this case.

 

The best treatment for opioid overdose is naloxone, which is an opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses the effects of opioids, including respiratory depression and sedation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Flumazenil: This is an antidote for benzodiazepine overdose, which may also cause sedation and respiratory depression. However, benzodiazepine overdose is less likely to cause such a severe decrease in respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils. The clinical presentation here is more consistent with opioid overdose.

 

Option C. Naltrexone: Naltrexone is also an opioid antagonist, but it is used for long-term management of opioid dependence, not for the acute reversal of opioid overdose. Naloxone is the preferred treatment in emergency situations.

 

Option D. N-Acetylcysteine: This is the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning, which does not fit the clinical picture described. Acetaminophen overdose typically presents with liver toxicity and elevated liver enzymes, not with respiratory depression or miosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The best treatment for a suspected opioid overdose is naloxone, which rapidly reverses the life-threatening effects of opioids, particularly respiratory depression and altered consciousness. Naloxone should be administered immediately in cases where opioid overdose is suspected, as it can be life-saving.

questions.stem: Amongst the options given below, which of these are not seen in cocaine poisoning?

options.label: A
options.text: Tingling and numbness of hands and feet

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Constricted pupils and bradycardia 

 

Cocaine is a powerful sympathomimetic drug that stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to the characteristic effects of increased heart rate (tachycardia), dilated pupils (mydriasis), hypertension, and hyperthermia. Cocaine poisoning is associated with increased adrenergic activity, which causes dilated pupils (mydriasis) and tachycardia, not constricted pupils (miosis) or bradycardia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tingling and numbness of hands and feet: This can be seen in cocaine use due to its effects on nerve conduction and potential vascular compromise, leading to tingling or numbness in the extremities.

 

Option C. Hypertension: Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that causes vasoconstriction and results in hypertension. This is a common finding in cases of cocaine poisoning.

 

Option D. Hyperthermia: Cocaine can increase metabolic rate and cause hyperthermia, which can be dangerous and lead to complications like seizures or rhabdomyolysis in severe cases.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cocaine poisoning is characterized by sympathomimetic effects such as tachycardia, mydriasis (dilated pupils), hypertension, and hyperthermia. Constricted pupils (miosis) and bradycardia are not seen in cocaine poisoning and are more characteristic of opioid or cholinergic toxicity.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with agitation, dilated pupils, and tachycardia. He appears restless and paranoid, and he is sweating profusely. His blood pressure is elevated. What is the likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Acute Cocaine poisoning

 

The symptoms described—agitation, dilated pupils (mydriasis), tachycardia, paranoia, profuse sweating, and elevated blood pressure—are classic signs of acute cocaine poisoning. Cocaine is a sympathomimetic drug that inhibits the reuptake of the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, leading to heightened adrenergic activity. This results in increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, agitation, and dilated pupils.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute Opioid overdose: Opioid overdose typically causes CNS depression, with symptoms like miosis (constricted pupils), bradycardia, and respiratory depression—none of which match the patient's presentation.

 

Option B. Acute Benzodiazepine overdose: Benzodiazepine overdose generally leads to sedation, CNS depression, and hypotension, not the agitation, tachycardia, and dilated pupils seen here.

 

Option D. Acute Alcohol intoxication: Acute alcohol intoxication may cause slurred speech, ataxia, and impaired judgment, but it does not typically result in the sympathomimetic effects (agitation, tachycardia, and dilated pupils) seen with cocaine poisoning.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cocaine poisoning presents with sympathomimetic features such as agitation, tachycardia, dilated pupils, elevated blood pressure, and profuse sweating due to the inhibition of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin reuptake. Recognizing these signs is crucial in differentiating cocaine toxicity from other overdoses such as opioids or benzodiazepines, which typically cause CNS depression.

questions.stem: Activated charcoal is ineffective in poisoning of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ethyl alcohol

 

Activated charcoal works by adsorbing toxins in the gastrointestinal tract and is commonly used for treating many types of poisonings. However, it is ineffective against certain substances, including ethyl alcohol, because alcohol is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and does not bind well to activated charcoal. Other substances that activated charcoal is ineffective against include metals, hydrocarbons, acids, alkalis, and certain chemicals like cyanide and organophosphates.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acetaminophen: Activated charcoal is effective in acetaminophen poisoning, as it can adsorb the drug in the gastrointestinal tract and prevent its further absorption.

 

Option B. Phenothiazines: Activated charcoal is effective in cases of phenothiazine poisoning (a class of antipsychotic drugs), as it can bind these drugs and reduce their absorption.

 

Option C. Barbiturates: Activated charcoal is also effective in barbiturate poisoning and may be used to prevent further absorption, especially if administered early.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Activated charcoal is ineffective in the treatment of ethyl alcohol poisoning because alcohol does not bind to charcoal. Activated charcoal is commonly used for various other poisonings, but it does not work for substances like alcohol, metals, organophosphates, and hydrocarbons. Recognizing when activated charcoal is appropriate or ineffective is essential in managing poisoning cases.

questions.stem: A Casualty medical officer is called to assess a patient who has ingested a toxic substance. During the assessment, the medical officer observes that the patient's urine has turned green. This unusual symptom raises concerns about the specific toxic substance involved. Which toxic substance is most likely responsible for the green-colored urine seen in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Phenol

 

Phenol (carbolic acid) poisoning is known to cause green-colored urine (also referred to as carboluria). This happens because phenol is metabolized into hydroquinone and pyrocatechol, which can cause the characteristic green discoloration of the urine. Phenol can also lead to tissue accumulation, resulting in a condition called sucrosis (a blackish discoloration), but green urine is a key symptom of phenol poisoning.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lead: Lead poisoning does not typically cause green urine. It may result in other symptoms such as anemia, abdominal pain, and neurological symptoms but not this specific change in urine color.

 

Option C. Organophosphorus: Organophosphorus poisoning leads to cholinergic symptoms such as salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, and muscle twitching but does not cause green-colored urine.

 

Option D. Cyanide: Cyanide poisoning is associated with symptoms like respiratory failure and cherry-red skin, but it does not cause a change in urine color to green.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Green-colored urine in a poisoning case is characteristic of phenol (carbolic acid) poisoning, which causes the breakdown products hydroquinone and pyrocatechol to be excreted in the urine. Recognizing such distinctive signs is important for the diagnosis and management of specific toxic ingestions.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with symptoms of poisoning. He is conscious but in distress, and reports ingesting a substance about an hour ago. The medical officer notes a distinct smell from the patient's breath. Considering the nature of the substance ingested and the time since ingestion, the medical officer must decide on the appropriate decontamination procedure. For which of the following poisons, consistent with the patient's presentation, is gastric lavage particularly indicated?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Carbolic acid

 

Gastric lavage is generally contraindicated in cases of corrosive poisonings (such as sulfuric acid, oxalic acid, and caustic potash) due to the risk of further damaging the gastrointestinal tract, which can lead to perforation. However, carbolic acid (phenol) is an exception because it causes tissue hardening (known as coagulative necrosis) rather than the liquefaction necrosis caused by other corrosive agents. This hardening effect reduces the risk of perforation, making gastric lavage a safe option for decontamination in cases of carbolic acid poisoning.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Oxalic acid: Gastric lavage is contraindicated for oxalic acid poisoning due to its corrosive effects on the gastrointestinal tract and the risk of perforation.

 

Option C. Sulfuric acid: Sulfuric acid is a strong corrosive that can cause severe burns to the gastrointestinal mucosa, making gastric lavage unsafe due to the risk of perforation.

 

Option D. Caustic potash: Caustic potash (potassium hydroxide) is a highly corrosive alkali, and gastric lavage is contraindicated because of the potential to cause further damage to the already compromised gastrointestinal lining.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gastric lavage is contraindicated in most cases of corrosive poisoning due to the risk of perforation; however, it can be considered in carbolic acid poisoning because of its unique property of coagulative necrosis, which reduces the risk of perforation. Recognizing when gastric lavage is appropriate is crucial for managing poisoning cases safely.

questions.stem: A person was brought to emergency with history of snake bite 8 hours ago. The patient had low respiratory rate and bradycardia with drooping of eyelids noted. 10 vials of antivenom were administered. What is the next line of management?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Give atropine + neostigmine

 

The symptoms of drooping eyelids (ptosis), low respiratory rate, and bradycardia suggest the effects of neurotoxic snake venom, likely from a snake such as a cobra or krait, which causes neuromuscular blockade. The administration of atropine + neostigmine is appropriate for managing neurotoxic effects, particularly to reverse the effects of venom-induced paralysis.

 

  • Atropine is used to counteract the bradycardia, while neostigmine (a cholinesterase inhibitor) helps by increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, improving muscle strength and reversing the effects of neurotoxic venom.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Check for blood coagulation profile: This would be more relevant in cases of hemotoxic snake bites (e.g., viper bites) that affect the clotting system. However, in this case, the neurotoxic symptoms indicate that neurotoxic management is more urgent.

 

Option C. IV hydrocortisone: Corticosteroids are sometimes used in allergic reactions but are not part of the standard management of neurotoxic snake bites. They do not address the primary issue of neurotoxicity.

 

Option D. Inj epinephrine: Epinephrine is used to treat anaphylactic reactions or severe allergic responses, which are not indicated in this scenario. There is no indication that the patient is experiencing an allergic reaction to the antivenom or snake bite.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of neurotoxic snake bites, presenting with symptoms like ptosis, bradycardia, and respiratory depression, the administration of atropine + neostigmine is critical after antivenom to reverse neurotoxic paralysis.

questions.stem: After visiting a village temple with his grandmother, a 5-year-old boy began crying intensely during the return trip. Within three hours, he was brought to the emergency department. He displayed symptoms such as altered consciousness, cold and sweaty extremities, heightened salivation, and excessive sweating. Physical examination revealed paleness and priapism, along with vital signs as follows: blood pressure of 140/78 mmHg, heart rate of 152 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 96%. Considering his condition, what treatment approach would you choose for his management?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Prazosin

 

The presentation is consistent with a scorpion sting, which causes autonomic storm due to the release of massive amounts of catecholamines and other neurotoxins. The child has tachycardia, excessive sweating, hypertension, and priapism, all hallmark signs of a scorpion sting's systemic effects.

 

The treatment of choice for managing the adrenergic storm in scorpion stings is prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker. Prazosin helps counteract the excessive catecholamine activity and effectively lowers blood pressure, improves blood circulation, and reduces systemic symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anti-snake venom: This would be indicated for a snake bite, but the symptoms in this case (high heart rate, hypertension, priapism) suggest a scorpion sting rather than a snake bite.

 

Option B. Methylprednisolone: Steroids are used in various inflammatory conditions but are not the first-line treatment for scorpion stings or catecholamine storm.

 

Option D. Adrenaline: Adrenaline is used in anaphylaxis and other emergencies but would worsen the patient's condition by further stimulating catecholamine release, exacerbating the symptoms of a scorpion sting.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of scorpion sting with symptoms of catecholamine excess (e.g., tachycardia, hypertension, priapism, excessive sweating), the treatment of choice is prazosin to counteract the effects of the catecholamine surge. Recognizing these signs and treating promptly with the appropriate antidote is crucial to managing scorpion envenomation effectively.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old individual presents to the emergency department with severe pain, restlessness, hypertension, tachycardia, and sweating after being stung by a scorpion. The sting site is red and swollen, with no signs of necrosis. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the sting site

options.label: D
options.text: Cleanse the wound and apply ice packs

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Administer prazosin

 

This patient presents with symptoms consistent with a scorpion sting that has triggered a catecholamine storm, leading to hypertension, tachycardia, and sweating. The appropriate treatment for managing the adrenergic crisis induced by scorpion venom is prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, which counteracts the effects of excessive catecholamine release and stabilizes the patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Administer antivenom immediately: Antivenom is not typically required in most scorpion stings unless there are severe, life-threatening systemic symptoms or the species of scorpion is particularly dangerous. In this case, the patient's systemic symptoms are best managed with prazosin.

 

Option B. Apply a tourniquet proximal to the sting site: Applying a tourniquet is not recommended for scorpion stings, as it may worsen the local effects and lead to ischemia without effectively controlling the venom's spread.

 

Option D. Cleanse the wound and apply ice packs: While cleansing the wound is important for preventing infection, it does not address the systemic effects of the scorpion venom, which are the primary concern in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For patients presenting with systemic symptoms of catecholamine excess after a scorpion sting, the primary treatment is prazosin. It effectively counters the adrenergic storm caused by the venom, leading to symptom resolution and stabilization.

questions.stem: A 35-year industrial worker presents with severe burns on his hands and arms after a workplace accident. There are deep burns with extensive tissue dissolution. Burns appear slimy, slippery, and gelatinous. Likely responsible agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Sodium hydroxide

 

The described burns, including tissue dissolution, slimy, and gelatinous appearance, are indicative of liquefactive necrosis, which is typically caused by alkali substances like sodium hydroxide (NaOH). Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis by breaking down cell membranes and dissolving proteins, leading to deep tissue damage.

 

  • L for Liquefactive, L for Alkalis: Alkali substances penetrate deeply into tissues and cause extensive damage, which explains the tissue dissolution and slimy appearance of the burns in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydrochloric acid, Option B. Nitric acid and Option C. Sulfuric acid: Acids typically cause coagulative necrosis, which results in tissue hardening and a leathery appearance. Acids cause surface burns by denaturing proteins, but they do not cause the liquefactive necrosis seen in alkali burns.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Alkalis like sodium hydroxide cause liquefactive necrosis, leading to deep tissue damage with a slimy and gelatinous appearance. In contrast, acids cause coagulative necrosis. Recognizing the type of necrosis can help in identifying the responsible chemical agent in burn injuries.

questions.stem: A patient was brought to casualty with seizures. He had multiple episodes and was taking herbal medicines for the same. He was conscious in between the episodes. During the episodes, he had arching of his back. What is the likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Strychnine

 

The patient's presentation of multiple seizures, consciousness between episodes, and arching of the back (opisthotonos) strongly suggests strychnine poisoning. Strychnine is a potent neurotoxin that causes exaggerated reflex responses by blocking the inhibitory neurotransmitter glycine in the spinal cord, leading to muscle spasms and convulsions while the patient remains fully conscious during the episodes.

 

  • Strychnine poisoning is characterized by muscle rigidity, severe spasms, and opisthotonos (arching of the back), with the patient often remaining conscious between episodes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ricinus: Ricinus (castor bean) poisoning typically leads to gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, but not the specific seizure pattern or opisthotonos seen in this case.

 

Option C. Nerium odorum: Poisoning with Nerium odorum (oleander) primarily affects the cardiac system, causing arrhythmias, bradycardia, and gastrointestinal symptoms, but not seizures with opisthotonos.

 

Option D. Datura: Datura poisoning (anticholinergic toxicity) can cause delirium, hallucinations, and tachycardia, but it does not typically present with the seizure pattern or opisthotonos described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Strychnine poisoning causes muscle rigidity, spasms, and seizures while the patient remains conscious during the episodes, often presenting with arching of the back (opisthotonos). Recognizing these symptoms is crucial in diagnosing strychnine toxicity and differentiating it from other toxicological emergencies.

questions.stem: A 25-year male presents after ingesting oxalic acid. He has severe burning pain in throat and difficulty breathing. His BP is normal but appears restless. Lab tests reveal metabolic acidosis. Most appropriate immediate intervention?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Endotracheal intubation 

 

The most critical issue in this case is the patient's airway and breathing. Oxalic acid is a corrosive substance, and ingestion can cause severe damage to the mucosal lining of the throat and respiratory tract, leading to airway obstruction. The patient is already showing signs of difficulty breathing, and the first priority is to secure the airway. Endotracheal intubation should be performed immediately to maintain an open airway and ensure the patient can breathe properly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Administration of IV calcium gluconate: This may be useful later to address hypocalcemia caused by oxalic acid binding to calcium, but it is not the immediate priority in managing the airway.

 

Option C. Administration of activated charcoal: Activated charcoal is ineffective for caustic substances like oxalic acid, and it is not recommended in corrosive poisonings because it does not neutralize the acid or prevent damage.

 

Option D. Immediate induction of vomiting: Vomiting is contraindicated in cases of corrosive poisoning, as it can cause further damage to the esophagus and throat due to the corrosive nature of the substance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of corrosive poisoning, the primary concern is ensuring airway patency and breathing. Immediate management should focus on securing the airway, often requiring endotracheal intubation, especially if there are signs of respiratory difficulty.

questions.stem: In OPC poisoning, treatment was done with atropine and pralidoxime. Hyperthermia occurs. What could be the cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atropine Toxicity

 

Atropine is an anticholinergic drug used in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning to counteract the effects of excessive acetylcholine. However, excessive doses of atropine can lead to atropine toxicity, which includes symptoms of anticholinergic syndrome such as hyperthermia (due to reduced sweating), tachycardia, dry skin, flushing, and confusion.

 

In OPC poisoning, the cholinergic effects cause excessive sweating and a decrease in body temperature. When atropine is administered in large doses, the opposite effect occurs: inhibition of sweating leads to hyperthermia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aspiration Pneumonia: While this is a potential complication of OPC poisoning, it would not directly cause hyperthermia. It would more likely lead to respiratory symptoms.

 

Option C. Oximes toxicity: Oximes (e.g., pralidoxime) are used to reactivate cholinesterase but are not commonly associated with hyperthermia as a side effect.

 

Option D. Cyanosis: Cyanosis refers to a bluish discoloration due to inadequate oxygenation and is unrelated to hyperthermia. It would not cause an increase in body temperature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Atropine toxicity can cause hyperthermia due to its anticholinergic effects, which inhibit sweating and increase body temperature. In the treatment of OPC poisoning, careful monitoring of atropine dosage is essential to avoid these toxic effects.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male arrives in the emergency department after being exposed to an unidentified toxic substance given to him by a friend. His symptoms include dry mouth, urinary retention, and constipation. During the examination, his pulse rate is recorded at 140 beats per minute, and his pupils are observed to be dilated. Which substance is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Belladona

 

The patient's symptoms of dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia (pulse rate of 140 bpm), and dilated pupils are classic signs of anticholinergic toxicity. Belladonna (Atropa belladonna) is an anticholinergic agent, and ingestion of substances derived from it (or similar plants like Datura) leads to these symptoms due to the blockade of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.

 

Anticholinergic symptoms are often summarized as:

 

  • Dry as a bone (dry mouth, reduced sweating)
  • Blind as a bat (dilated pupils, blurred vision)
  • Red as a beet (flushed skin)
  • Mad as a hatter (confusion, hallucinations)
  • Hot as a hare (hyperthermia)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Heroin and Option B. Morphine: Both are CNS depressants (opioids) and would typically cause miosis (constricted pupils), sedation, and respiratory depression, not the anticholinergic effects described here.

 

Option C. Malathion: Malathion is an organophosphate (cholinergic poison), which would lead to increased secretions, bradycardia, constricted pupils, diarrhea, and urinary frequency—the opposite of the dry, anticholinergic symptoms seen in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Belladonna (Atropa belladonna) and related plants cause anticholinergic toxicity, which manifests as dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia, and dilated pupils. Recognizing these signs is crucial for diagnosing anticholinergic poisoning and differentiating it from other toxic exposures like opioids or cholinergic agents.
